analysis.one_liner: Raises the debt limit in exchange for spending cuts, work requirements, student-loan relief repeal, and expanded oil and gas leasing.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 217-215 with no Democratic support on April 26, 2023, but the Senate never voted, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have suspended the federal debt limit through March 31, 2024, or until the debt rose by $1.5 trillion, whichever came first. To get that increase, it capped domestic spending for a decade, expanded work requirements for food stamps, Medicaid, and welfare, canceled student-loan relief, rescinded IRS enforcement funding, repealed most clean-energy tax credits, and opened federal land to expanded oil, gas, coal, and mining development with fewer environmental reviews and lower royalties. [S2] [S3] [S4]
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, and coal companies gain the most: the bill mandates frequent lease sales on federal land and offshore, repeals the royalty and fee increases enacted in 2022, short-circuits environmental reviews, and limits court challenges. Wealthy households and large filers gain from rescinded IRS enforcement funding. Defense-favored appropriators gain from the debt-limit increase paired with cuts elsewhere. An increase in the debt limit also would have avoided a federal default, which benefits everyone.

how_it_helps.text: Suspends the debt limit through March 31, 2024, or until debt increases by $1.5 trillion, whichever comes first.

Requires Interior to hold at least four oil and gas lease sales in each state with land available for leasing and at least two annual sales in Gulf of Mexico and Alaska offshore planning areas, and repeals the royalty and fee increases enacted in the Inflation Reduction Act.
Repeals or shortens dozens of clean-energy tax credits, including credits for wind, solar, electric vehicles, clean hydrogen, nuclear, sustainable aviation fuel, and clean fuels.

Rescinds unobligated COVID-19 funds and unobligated Inflation Reduction Act funds, and rescinds the IRS enforcement and operations funding provided in 2022, including funding for a report on a free direct e-file tax return system.
Caps discretionary spending at set dollar amounts for fiscal years 2024 through 2033, which the summary describes as decreases in discretionary spending.

analysis.who_pays: Low-income households bear the largest costs: SNAP work rules would extend to adults up to age 56, Medicaid would impose 80-hour monthly work requirements with disenrollment for noncompliance, and TANF rules tighten. Student borrowers would lose the payment pause, debt discharge, and new income-driven repayment plan. Everyone who pays taxes honestly pays when IRS enforcement is cut, because unpaid taxes by high earners go uncollected. Clean-energy consumers and workers lose tax credits, prevailing-wage requirements, and the low-income solar and wind credit bonus. Lower royalties mean less money flowing back to the Treasury and land and conservation funds.

drawbacks.text: The bill expands SNAP work requirements to adults up to age 56 and imposes an 80-hour monthly work requirement on adults ages 19-55 in Medicaid, allowing states to disenroll people who do not meet it for three or more months a year, cutting off food and health coverage for people who trip on paperwork rather than on willingness to work.

It nullifies the student-loan payment suspension, the debt-discharge action, and the new income-driven repayment rule, and bars the Education Department from issuing substantially similar actions unless Congress expressly authorizes them.
It rescinds IRS enforcement funding, leaving less money to audit high-income and complex returns and shrinking revenue that offsets the deficit.

It sharply narrows environmental review of energy and mining projects, limits who can sue and when, and bars courts from halting projects except for imminent and substantial environmental harm, leaving communities near pipelines, mines, and lease sites with less recourse.

It would require Congress to approve every 'major rule' before it takes effect, letting a single chamber's inaction block health, safety, and financial regulations that agencies have studied and finalized.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Raising the debt limit was genuinely necessary to avoid a default that would have hurt everyone, and deficit reduction is a legitimate goal. But this package tied the increase to cuts aimed overwhelmingly at low-income households, a hollowing out of IRS enforcement that mainly protects high earners, and a wish list for extractive industries that gives away public resources at lower royalty rates. An honest supporter would also acknowledge the bill was written as an opening position for debt-limit negotiations rather than as legislation meant to become law, and indeed it never received a Senate vote.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a narrow party-line vote (217-215), but the Senate placed it on its calendar, held committee hearings, and never brought it to a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced April 25, 2023, and the House passed it the next day, 217-215, with 217 Republicans voting yes and zero Democrats.
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill to committee failed 211-221, with every voting Democrat in favor and every voting Republican opposed.
The Senate received the bill on May 1, 2023, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 41.
The Senate Budget Committee held hearings on the bill on May 4, 2023, but the Senate never voted on passage.
No further action occurred for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025, so the bill never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people who would have lost under the bill are better off that it died: SNAP and Medicaid recipients, student borrowers, workers on clean-energy projects, and agencies that keep unspent IRS and community-grant funding. Oil, gas, and mining companies did not get the expanded access and lower royalties the bill offered, though the debt-limit standoff it fueled shaped later negotiations.

for.name: Jodey C. Arrington
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as the Republican opening proposal for raising the debt limit.

for.name: 217 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, supplying every vote for the bill.

for.name: Kevin McCarthy
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under a rule one day after introduction and used it as the Republican's starting position in debt-limit negotiations with the White House.

against.name: 211 of 216 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage and voted yes on the motion to recommit the bill to committee.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Declined to schedule the bill for a Senate vote, calling it dead on arrival, leaving it on the calendar.

against.name: Joe Biden
against.what_they_did: Publicly threatened to veto the bill and refused to negotiate over the debt limit on those terms.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost entirely by party: 217 of 222 voting Republicans voted yes while 211 of 213 voting Democrats voted no, with four Republicans and two absent Democrats accounting for the exceptions.

industries.note: The bill mandates quarterly onshore lease sales with at least four sales per eligible state, requires annual offshore sales in the Gulf and Alaska, repeals the 2022 royalty and fee increases, and speeds permits while narrowing environmental review and lawsuits. Companies get more access to public land and water while paying less back to the Treasury, and the air and water near drilling sites get less protection.

The bill nullifies the paused federal coal program review, grants pending coal leases, treats mineral projects as expedited 'covered projects,' and extends streamlined permitting to all minerals, not just critical ones. Miners gain faster permits on public land with fewer checks on pollution and land damage.

industries.industry: Clean energy, electric vehicle, and battery industries
industries.note: The bill repeals or terminates credits for wind, solar, storage, electric vehicles, clean hydrogen, nuclear, sustainable aviation fuel, and clean fuels, and strips prevailing-wage and domestic-content conditions. Repealing these credits raises the cost of clean energy for consumers and workers as well as the companies that sell it.

Rescinding the 2022 IRS enforcement funding means fewer audits of complex, high-dollar returns. The revenue the government would have collected goes uncollected, so compliant taxpayers effectively subsidize those who underpay.
The bill rescinds the IRS funding for a report on a free direct e-file system, keeping a government-run free filing option further from reality and preserving paid preparers' customer base.
